amor-fati: Amor fati, Latin for 'love of fate,' is Nietzsche's ideal of affirming your life completely — embracing not just its joys but its suffering, losses, and mistakes as necessary to it, rather than wishing any of it different. It goes beyond resignation: on this view, to love fate is to say yes to everything that has happened to you as if you had chosen it yourself.
animal-rights: Animal rights is the view that many nonhuman animals have moral claims on us that should not simply be traded away for human benefits. On the influential 'subject-of-a-life' view, any being with experiences, memories, and a life that matters to it has value of its own — not merely value as a resource — so using or harming it requires a justification, not just habit or species membership.
applied-ethics: Applied ethics is the branch of philosophy that brings moral theories to bear on concrete practical problems — in medicine, technology, war, business, and AI. Instead of asking only, in the abstract, what makes an action right, it asks whether genetic engineering is permissible, when lying is wrong, or how we should treat intelligent machines. It tests principles against hard cases, and lets hard cases refine the principles.
aristotle-friendship: For Aristotle, friendship (philia) is essential to the good life — no one, he says, would choose to live without friends. He distinguishes friendships based on usefulness, friendships based on pleasure, and the best kind: between virtuous people who wish each other well for their own sake. Such friendship, he argues, mirrors how we value ourselves and helps both friends grow in virtue.
binary-oppositions: A binary opposition is a pair of contrasted terms — nature/culture, reason/emotion, us/them — through which, structuralists argue, we organize meaning: we grasp each side partly by what it is not. Critics add that such pairs are rarely neutral; they tend to smuggle in hierarchy, ranking one side above the other, and the boundary between them often proves unstable once examined closely.
categorical-imperative: Kant's categorical imperative is his supreme principle of morality: act only on rules that you could rationally will everyone to follow. Unlike advice that depends on your goals ('if you want to stay fit, exercise'), it commands unconditionally — hence 'categorical.' Famously, it makes lying wrong even when convenient, because you cannot coherently will a world where everyone lies whenever it suits them.
consequentialism: Consequentialism is the view that the morality of an action depends entirely on its results: an act is right if it produces the best overall outcome. Its most famous form, utilitarianism, says the best outcome is the one with the greatest total happiness. Opponents object that this seems to permit sacrificing individuals for the greater good — a challenge that shapes much modern ethics.
death-of-god: Nietzsche's 'death of God' is not a claim that a divine being literally died, but a diagnosis: belief in the Christian God — and with it any single, objective foundation for values — has become incredible to modern culture. The fear is nihilism: without that foundation, our highest values lose their grounding. Nietzsche's challenge is whether we can create new values rather than despair.
deconstruction: Deconstruction, associated with the philosopher Jacques Derrida, is a way of reading that looks for how a text undermines its own stated meaning. It shows that the distinctions a text relies on — speech over writing, reason over emotion — are unstable, since each term secretly depends on the one it excludes. Contrary to stereotype, it is careful reading, not destruction: it exposes tensions already inside the work.
deep-ecology: Deep ecology, founded by the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess, holds that nature has value in its own right, not merely as a resource for humans. It rejects the human-centered outlook that ranks people above other living things and calls instead for a wider sense of self — seeing oneself as part of the living world — so that protecting nature comes to feel like protecting oneself.
deontology: Deontology is the family of moral views on which some actions are required or forbidden in themselves, regardless of their consequences. On this picture, morality is a matter of duties — not lying, keeping promises, respecting persons — and you may not wrong one person even to prevent greater harm elsewhere. Its best-known defender is Kant, who grounded duty in respect for rational beings.
dichotomy-of-control: The Stoic philosopher Epictetus taught a simple division: some things are 'up to us' — our judgments, desires, and actions — while others are not, including health, wealth, reputation, and other people's behavior. On this view, disturbance comes from worrying about what we cannot control; tranquility comes from focusing our effort only on what we can, and accepting the rest with equanimity.
epicurean-death: The ancient philosopher Epicurus argued that 'death is nothing to us': when we exist, death has not yet arrived, and when death arrives, we no longer exist to suffer it. Since we never actually experience being dead, he held, death cannot harm us — and fearing it is irrational. Critics reply that death can still deprive us of future goods we would otherwise have enjoyed.
epicurean-pleasure: Epicurus made pleasure the goal of life, but his menu is modest: real pleasure is the absence of bodily pain and mental anxiety — a tranquil state the Greeks called ataraxia. He counseled limiting our desires to what is natural and necessary (food, friendship, thought) and forgoing luxuries and ambitions whose pursuit breeds anxiety. Prudence, on this view, matters more than indulgence.
existence-risk: An existential risk is a danger that could annihilate humanity or permanently destroy its potential — nuclear war, engineered pandemics, runaway artificial intelligence, environmental collapse. Philosophers who study it argue that extinction is categorically worse than any catastrophe that spares survivors, because it forecloses all future generations and everything they might achieve. Reducing such risks, they contend, may be the defining task of our century.
fascism: Fascism is a far-right political ideology that elevates the nation or race above the individual, celebrates strength and struggle, and demands a strong leader and a single party with unchecked power. Historical fascism, as in Mussolini's Italy and Nazi Germany, crushed dissent, attacked liberal democracy, and glorified war. Because regimes vary, many scholars describe it as a cluster of traits rather than one fixed doctrine.
grand-narratives: Jean-François Lyotard defined the postmodern condition as 'incredulity toward grand narratives.' Grand narratives are the big, all-embracing stories societies once used to give meaning and legitimacy — history as progress, science as universal enlightenment, emancipation through revolution. Lyotard thought these had lost their credibility, leaving only smaller, local stories. Critics note a paradox: rejecting all grand stories can itself become one.
kant-humanity-formula: Kant's 'Formula of Humanity' says: treat every person — yourself included — always as an end in themselves, never merely as a means. People, unlike tools, have absolute worth and purposes of their own, so it is wrong to use, deceive, or coerce them just to advance your goals. The violation is often subtler than violence: it happens whenever consent is bypassed or trust exploited.
ockham-razor: Ockham's razor is a rule of thumb for choosing between theories, named after the medieval philosopher William of Ockham: when rival explanations account for the facts equally well, prefer the one that makes fewer assumptions or posits fewer entities. It is a principle of parsimony, not a proof — simplicity guides plausibility, and an overzealous razor can cut away the true explanation along with the extravagant ones.
plato-justice: In Plato's Republic, justice is the order in which each part does its proper work: in the city, rulers, guardians, and producers each performing their role; in the soul, reason ruling spirit and appetite. Plato argues justice is not merely advantageous but good in itself — the just person's soul is harmonious and happy, even if the world mistreats them — his answer to those who claim injustice pays better.
problem-of-evil: The problem of evil is the classic challenge to belief in God: if God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good, why do innocent people and animals suffer so terribly? Responses ('theodicies') claim that evil serves greater goods, such as free will or moral growth, or that God's reasons may be beyond our understanding. Critics counter that the sheer scale of apparently pointless suffering makes such explanations hard to believe.
sisyphus: In Camus's essay The Myth of Sisyphus, the figure condemned to roll his boulder uphill forever embodies the 'absurd': the clash between our hunger for meaning and a universe that offers none. Camus argues against both despair and false consolation. Sisyphus's conscious defiance — owning his fate and finding his struggle enough — makes him an absurd hero: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.'
supererogation: Supererogation refers to acts that go 'beyond the call of duty': morally admirable and praiseworthy, yet not required — like donating an organ to a stranger or running into a burning building. The category raises puzzles: if morality demands only the ordinary, what makes saints and heroes praiseworthy for doing more? Some ethicists doubt the category entirely, holding that if an act is morally best, it becomes obligatory.
thoreau-walden: Walden (1854) is Henry David Thoreau's account of the two years he spent living simply in a cabin near Walden Pond. Meant as an experiment rather than hermitage, the book argues that most people rush through 'lives of quiet desperation' chasing possessions; by simplifying — fewer wants, close attention to nature — one gains time, freedom, and depth. It remains a touchstone for deliberate living and environmental thought.
